lessons.title: Describing Systems: Block Diagrams, Schematics and Flowcharts

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a system block diagram?
A) A diagram using standard electrical component symbols to show how parts are wired
B) A diagram using labelled rectangles and arrows to show how sub-systems are linked
C) A diagram using ovals and diamonds to show the sequence of steps in a process
D) A photograph of a product showing all its internal components
practice_questions.marks: B) A diagram using labelled rectangles and arrows to show how sub-systems are linked [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between an open-loop control system and a closed-loop control system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct difference, up to 2 marks:
- Open-loop has no feedback path; closed-loop has a feedback path that monitors the output.
- Open-loop output cannot correct itself if conditions change; closed-loop adjusts the process to match the desired output.
- Open-loop is simpler/cheaper to build; closed-loop is more accurate but more complex.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A designer is creating a block diagram for an automatic greenhouse temperature control system. The system uses a temperature sensor, a microcontroller and a fan motor.

Name the correct flowchart symbol for each of the following:
(a) START
(b) “Read temperature sensor”
(c) “Is temperature above 25°C?”
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Oval / terminator [1 mark]
(b) Rectangle / process box [1 mark]
(c) Diamond / decision box [1 mark]
[3 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Vantage Control Ltd is designing an automated paint-mixing machine. The machine reads a colour code from a barcode, mixes the correct pigments and fills a tin.

Draw and label a system block diagram for this machine. Your diagram should show at least three sub-systems and indicate the direction of signal flow.
practice_questions.type: 5 marks — Complete the Flowchart or System Diagram
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for the following:
- INPUT sub-system correctly labelled (e.g. barcode scanner / colour code input) [1 mark]
- At least one PROCESS sub-system correctly labelled (e.g. microcontroller / mixing controller) [1 mark]
- OUTPUT sub-system correctly labelled (e.g. pigment valves / tin-filling actuator) [1 mark]
- Arrows showing correct direction of signal/material flow between blocks [1 mark]
- Diagram uses rectangles only (no component symbols, no flowchart shapes) [1 mark]
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a schematic drawing and a system block diagram. In your answer, state when an engineer would use each type.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A schematic uses standard component symbols (e.g. resistor zigzag, capacitor lines) to show how components are wired; a block diagram uses labelled rectangles to show how sub-systems are linked.
- A schematic is used when a technician needs to build or fault-find a circuit; a block diagram is used at the planning stage to show the overall system structure before detailed design.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Hartwell Automation Ltd manufactures industrial ovens used in a food factory. The oven must maintain a temperature of 180°C. A sensor inside the oven measures the actual temperature every 10 seconds and feeds the reading back to a controller, which switches the heating elements on or off as needed.

Evaluate whether a closed-loop or open-loop control system is the better choice for this oven. Use engineering reasoning to justify your answer.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Detailed comparison of open-loop and closed-loop systems applied to the oven context. Explains that open-loop (e.g. a fixed timer) would cause temperature drift if the ambient conditions change, door is opened or batch size varies, resulting in inconsistent food quality or safety hazards. Clearly explains how the closed-loop arrangement described (sensor feeds back to controller, controller switches heating) corrects deviations from 180°C automatically, ensuring consistent output. Considers a disadvantage of closed-loop (more complex, sensor can fail) and reaches a justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6): Correct identification of the system as closed-loop. Explains the benefit of feedback (auto-correction) and links it to the oven application. Some comparison with open-loop but may not fully develop the disadvantage or link to engineering consequences.

Developing (3-4): Describes the closed-loop system broadly. May correctly identify that feedback improves accuracy without explaining the mechanism. Limited comparison.

Emerging (1-2): Simple statement that closed-loop is better with minimal justification. May confuse open and closed loop.

[8 marks]

before.content_html:
Thinking in Systems

Every engineered product — from a car braking system to a factory conveyor — is a system. Engineers break complicated products down into smaller, manageable pieces so they can design, build and test each part separately. The three main tools for doing this are block diagrams, schematic drawings and flowcharts. Understanding when to use each one is essential.

Key Fact

The input–process–output (IPO) model is the foundation of all system design. Every system takes something in, does something to it, and produces a result. Identifying these three stages is the first step when analysing or designing any engineering system.

The Input–Process–Output Model

The input–process–output model (IPO) lets engineers describe any system with three boxes. In an electric kettle: the input is the mains electricity and cold water; the process is the heating element converting electrical energy to heat; the output is boiling water. In a car engine: the input is fuel and air; the process is combustion; the output is rotary motion at the crankshaft.

A system also has a system boundary — an imaginary line that separates what belongs to the system from the wider environment. Drawing the boundary forces the engineer to decide exactly what is and is not part of their design.

System Block Diagrams

A system block diagram uses rectangular blocks joined by arrows to show how sub-systems connect. Each block is labelled with what it does (e.g. “temperature sensor”, “microcontroller”, “motor driver”). The arrows show the direction of signal or energy flow.

Block diagrams are NOT circuit diagrams and NOT flowcharts. A circuit diagram shows how components are wired using standard symbols (resistor, capacitor, LED). A flowchart shows the sequence of steps a process or program follows. The examiner has repeatedly noted that students draw circuit diagrams when asked for block diagrams — these answers score zero.

Key Fact

A system block diagram uses labelled rectangles and arrows only — no component symbols (resistor zigzag, capacitor plates, logic gate shapes). If the diagram looks like a circuit, it is wrong. Blocks describe WHAT each sub-system does, not HOW it is built.

Open-Loop and Closed-Loop Control

In an open-loop system the output has no effect on the process. A toaster set to a timer is open-loop: it heats for a fixed time regardless of whether the toast is burnt or pale. In a closed-loop system a sensor monitors the output and feeds information back to the controller. An oven thermostat is closed-loop: it measures actual temperature and switches the heating element on or off to match the set point.

Closed-loop systems are more accurate but more complex to design. Most industrial control systems — from a car cruise-control to a furnace temperature controller — are closed-loop because small disturbances (draughts, varying load) would cause the output to drift without feedback correction.

Large systems are broken into sub-systems. A car has sub-systems for engine management, braking, steering, lighting, infotainment and climate control. Each sub-system can be designed and tested independently. On a block diagram, sub-systems are shown as blocks that can themselves be expanded into more detailed block diagrams — this is called hierarchical decomposition.

The system boundary decides what counts as an input and what counts as an output. For a car engine management sub-system, “throttle position” is an input (from outside the sub-system, controlled by the driver), whereas “fuel injector pulse width” is an output (leaving the sub-system to control the fuel delivery).

Schematic Drawings

A schematic drawing (or schematic) uses standard symbols to show how components connect, not how they are physically arranged on a PCB or in a machine. Electrical schematics use British Standard (BS 3939) symbols: zigzag for a resistor, two parallel lines for a capacitor, a circle with an arrow for a motor. Hydraulic and pneumatic schematics use ISO 1219 symbols: rectangles for cylinders, diamonds for filters, arrows on lines for flow direction.

Schematics are the standard language of engineering workshops. If you hand a schematic to a technician, they can identify every component and trace every connection regardless of what the physical product looks like. This is why drawing interpretation is a key skill examined in the written paper.

Flowcharts show the sequence of steps in a process or control program. There are four standard symbols you must know:

  • Terminator (oval) — marks the START or END of the process. Every flowchart must begin and end with a terminator.
  • Process box (rectangle) — shows an action to be carried out, e.g. “Switch motor ON” or “Heat element for 30 s”.
  • Input/Output parallelogram — shows data entering or leaving the system, e.g. “Read sensor value” or “Display temperature”.
  • Decision diamond — asks a YES/NO question, e.g. “Is temperature > 80°C?” with two arrow paths leaving it.

Feedback loops in flowcharts must loop back to a decision diamond or an earlier process box — never to the start terminator. A common error is drawing the feedback arrow going all the way back to START, creating an infinite loop with no way to exit.

Choosing the Right Representation

The examiner expects you to choose the correct type of diagram for the question. Use a block diagram when asked to show how sub-systems relate and where signals flow. Use a schematic when asked to show component connections using standard symbols. Use a flowchart when asked to show the sequence of steps or decisions in a process or control program. Mixing these up is one of the most common reasons students lose marks on systems questions.

lessons.title: Mechanical Systems: Motion, Linkages and Cams

before.content_html:
Four Types of Motion

Mechanical systems transmit and transform movement. Before designing a mechanism you must identify what type of motion is needed at the output. There are four types that engineers work with every day.

Rotary motion is spinning around a fixed axis — a motor shaft, a gear, a wheel. Linear motion is movement in a straight line, such as the travel of a drill bit moving into a workpiece. Reciprocating motion is back-and-forth movement along a straight line — a piston, a saw blade or a needle in an industrial sewing machine. Oscillating motion is a swinging or rocking motion around a fixed point, like a pendulum or a windscreen wiper arm.

In the examination you must use the correct technical terms — answers like “goes round and round” or “goes sideways” are not credited. A motor produces rotary motion; a piston produces reciprocating motion.

Key Fact

The four types of motion are rotary (spinning around an axis), linear (straight line), reciprocating (back-and-forth straight line) and oscillating (swinging around a fixed point). Most mechanisms convert one type of motion into another.

Linkages and Conversion of Motion

A linkage is a set of rigid bars joined by pivots that transmits or changes the direction of movement. Engineers use linkages when they need to transmit force around corners, reverse direction, or change the shape of a motion path.

The simplest linkage is a reverse linkage (bell crank). Pushing one arm down causes the other arm to push outward — the motion direction changes by 90°. Bicycle brake levers use this principle: squeezing the handle pulls a cable that pushes brake pads against the wheel rim. A parallel linkage keeps two bars moving in the same direction — used in toy train pantographs and car suspension systems.

The crank and slider mechanism is the fundamental converter of rotary motion into reciprocating motion. A rotating crank pin is connected to a slider (piston) by a connecting rod. As the crank rotates, the slider moves back and forth. Every internal combustion engine uses this principle — the rotating crankshaft drives the pistons up and down.

The reverse is also possible: a reciprocating steam engine drives a piston back and forth, which turns a crankshaft via a connecting rod to produce rotary motion at the wheels. Engineers describe this as converting reciprocating to rotary motion.

Cams and Followers

A cam is a specially shaped piece that rotates and pushes a component called a follower up and down as it turns. The key principle: the position of the follower at any instant depends entirely on the radius of the cam at the point of contact. Where the cam radius is large, the follower is pushed up. Where the radius is small, the follower drops down. This is the examiner’s most-tested cam concept — you must be able to explain it, not just name it.

Key Fact

The follower’s position at any moment is determined by the cam profile — specifically the radius of the cam at the point of contact. A large radius pushes the follower high; a small radius lets it drop. The cam profile is therefore what engineers adjust to control the follower’s movement pattern.

Four cam profiles appear in engineering exam questions:

  • Pear cam — egg-shaped profile. The follower rises slowly to a maximum height and then drops quickly. Used in car engine valve timing, where a valve must open slowly and snap shut.
  • Eccentric (circular) cam — a circular disc with the pivot offset from the centre. As it rotates the follower rises and falls smoothly in a simple harmonic pattern. Used in pumps and simple oscillating machines.
  • Snail (drop) cam — the follower rises very gradually around most of the rotation, then drops almost vertically as it reaches the “snail’s tail” drop. Used in clock escapements and stamping machines where a sudden downward force is needed.
  • Heart cam — heart-shaped profile that converts the continuous rotation into a back-and-forth motion of equal rate in both directions. Used in mechanisms where a constant-rate reciprocation is needed.

Choosing the Right Mechanism

When an engineer needs to convert motion, they select the mechanism based on the motion required and the forces involved. To convert rotary to reciprocating: use a cam or a crank and slider. To change the direction of a force: use a linkage (bell crank, reverse linkage). To transmit rotary motion between shafts that are far apart or at an angle: use gears, chains or belts (covered in Lesson 3).

At Rolls-Royce Turbine Assemblies in Derby, precision cams in the engine-control unit govern the opening and closing of fuel valves with timings accurate to thousandths of a second. The cam profile is machined to tolerances of ±0.005 mm because any deviation changes the valve timing and affects thrust output. This real-world context shows why understanding cam profiles matters beyond the classroom.

lessons.title: Mechanical Calculations: Gears, Pulleys and Mechanical Advantage

practice_questions.text: A gear train has a driver gear with 24 teeth and a driven gear with 96 teeth. Calculate the gear ratio.
practice_questions.marks:
Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth [1 mark for correct formula]
= 96 ÷ 24 [1 mark for correct substitution]
= 4:1 [1 mark for correct answer with ratio notation]
[3 marks — method marks awarded even if arithmetic error]
Note: accept 4 or 4.0 without ratio notation for 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
A workshop hoist uses a block-and-tackle with 5 rope sections to lift a heavy machine component weighing 1500 N.

(a) State the velocity ratio of the pulley system.
(b) Calculate the effort force required, assuming ideal (frictionless) conditions.
(c) Explain why the actual effort needed would be higher than your calculated value.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Calculation: Multi-Step with Unit Conversion
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Velocity ratio = 5 [1 mark]
(b) In ideal conditions MA = VR = 5
Effort = load ÷ MA = 1500 ÷ 5 = 300 N [1 mark for method, 1 mark for correct answer with unit]
(c) In a real system, friction in the pulleys and rope wastes energy, so more input force (effort) is required to move the same load / real MA is less than VR. [1 mark]
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Give two distinct reasons why a pulley system is used in a vehicle engine workshop to lift an engine out of a car.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct reason, up to 2 marks:
- It reduces the force (effort) needed to lift the heavy engine by multiplying the input force.
- It changes the direction of effort — the technician pulls down on the rope while the load moves upward.
- It allows a single person to lift a load that would otherwise require multiple people.
- It provides a controlled lift, reducing the risk of sudden movement.
[2 marks — must name the mechanism/benefit, not just 'easier' or 'quicker' alone]

practice_questions.text:
Norcroft Robotics Ltd designs a robotic arm. The arm joint is driven by an electric motor with a pinion gear of 15 teeth meshing with a large gear of 90 teeth. The large gear then meshes with a second pinion of 10 teeth, which drives a final output gear of 50 teeth.

Calculate the overall gear ratio of this compound gear train.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Calculation: Multi-Step with Unit Conversion
practice_questions.marks:
Stage 1 ratio = driven ÷ driver = 90 ÷ 15 = 6 [1 mark]
Stage 2 ratio = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 [1 mark]
Overall ratio = 6 × 5 = 30:1 [1 mark for method (multiply stages), 1 mark for correct answer]
[4 marks — method marks awarded for each stage even if overall answer wrong]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a ball bearing is used instead of a plain bearing in a high-speed electric motor shaft. Your answer should refer to the function of a ball bearing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A ball bearing uses rolling contact (steel balls in a hardened race) rather than sliding contact.
- Rolling contact significantly reduces friction between the rotating shaft and the housing.
- Less friction means lower energy losses as heat, longer component life, and the shaft can rotate at higher speeds without overheating.
[2 marks — answers that only say 'allows rotation' or 'spins' without mentioning friction reduction score zero]

practice_questions.text:
Harwick Elevators Ltd is designing a goods hoist for a warehouse. The engineers must choose between a chain-and-sprocket drive and a belt-and-pulley drive to transmit power from the motor to the lifting drum.

Evaluate which drive system is the better choice for this application. In your answer, consider the advantages and disadvantages of each system.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Detailed comparison of chain-and-sprocket vs belt-and-pulley. Chain: no slip (positive engagement with teeth), high load capacity, suitable for heavy goods hoist, needs lubrication, noisy, more expensive. Belt: quieter, cheaper, some slip possible under high load (safety benefit in a jam but reliability concern for a hoist), no lubrication needed, can accommodate slight misalignment. Evaluates each property against the warehouse goods hoist context (heavy loads, frequent use, reliability critical). Reaches a justified conclusion with engineering reasoning.

Secure (5-6): Identifies key differences (slip vs no-slip, lubrication, cost) and links at least two to the hoist context. Some evaluation but may not cover all relevant factors.

Developing (3-4): Describes one system more fully than the other. Limited comparison. May list properties without linking to the application.

Emerging (1-2): Basic description of one drive system with minimal comparison.

[8 marks]

before.content_html:
Two Types of Electrical Power

Every electrical system needs a power supply. In engineering there are two fundamentally different types: alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC).

UK mains electricity is 230 V AC at 50 Hz. The voltage swings between a positive peak and a negative peak 50 times per second, producing a smooth sine wave. If you display mains AC on an oscilloscope you see a repeating wave; if you display battery DC you see a flat horizontal line. Mains AC is used for high-power fixed equipment (motors, heaters, industrial machinery). Batteries produce DC and are used for portable, low-power and safety-critical applications.

Key Fact

Mains AC: 230 V, sine-wave waveform, high power, fixed location, not portable. Battery DC: typically 1.5–12 V, flat-line waveform, lower power, portable, finite energy store. Electronic circuits (microcontrollers, sensors, logic gates) require DC — a power supply unit (PSU) converts mains AC to regulated DC.

Transformers

A transformer changes the voltage of an AC supply. It consists of a primary coil (input) and a secondary coil (output) wound around a shared iron core. When AC flows in the primary coil, a changing magnetic field is created in the core; this induces a voltage in the secondary coil. Transformers only work with AC — a DC current creates a static magnetic field that induces nothing.

The relationship between voltages and number of turns is: $$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$$ where \(V_p\) is primary voltage, \(V_s\) is secondary voltage, \(N_p\) is number of primary turns and \(N_s\) is number of secondary turns.

Example: a transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. If the primary is connected to 230 V AC: $$V_s = \frac{V_p \times N_s}{N_p} = \frac{230 \times 100}{2000} = 11.5\text{ V}$$ This is a step-down transformer (output lower than input), used to produce safe low-voltage DC from mains. Step-up transformers increase voltage (more secondary turns than primary) and are used in electricity grid transmission.

A rectifier converts AC into DC. A single diode produces half-wave rectification — it blocks every negative half-cycle, leaving only the positive pulses. A bridge rectifier uses four diodes arranged in a diamond so that both the positive and negative half-cycles contribute to the output (full-wave rectification). The output is pulsing DC, which is smoothed by a capacitor to produce a steady DC voltage.

In practice, a mains-powered PSU contains a step-down transformer, a bridge rectifier and a smoothing capacitor — this chain produces the stable DC that electronic circuits need. Many also include a voltage-regulator IC to hold the output at an exact value (e.g. 5 V for a microcontroller).

Input Control Devices: Switches

A switch is the simplest input control device. Push-to-make switches (normally open) complete the circuit when pressed; push-to-break switches (normally closed) interrupt the circuit when pressed. Toggle switches, rotary switches and limit switches (triggered by a physical stop on a machine) are all common in engineering applications. Switches are direct inputs — they require a human or a mechanical actuator to operate them.

The Relay — Electrically Controlled Switch

A relay is an electromagnetic switch. A small current in the control coil creates a magnetic field that attracts an iron armature, closing (or opening) a separate set of contacts. The relay allows a low-voltage, low-current control signal (e.g. 5 V from a microcontroller) to switch a high-voltage, high-current circuit (e.g. 230 V AC motor). The two circuits are electrically isolated — a relay is the safe interface between control electronics and mains-powered equipment.

Key Fact

A relay uses a small control current to switch a large load current, and keeps the two circuits electrically isolated. This protects sensitive control electronics (microcontrollers, sensors) from the high voltages and currents of mains-powered output devices like motors and heaters.

Output devices convert electrical energy into other forms of energy. You need to know four types:

  • Electric motor — converts electrical energy into rotary mechanical energy. Used to drive pumps, conveyors, drills and fans. DC motors are common in battery-powered tools; AC motors power industrial machinery.
  • Solenoid — an electromagnet with a moveable iron core (plunger). When energised, the plunger is pulled into the coil, producing linear mechanical movement. Used in door locks, valve actuators and automatic dispensing machines. A solenoid converts electrical energy to linear mechanical motion.
  • Buzzer and bell — audible alarms that convert electrical energy to sound. A piezo buzzer uses a piezoelectric crystal that vibrates when current is applied. An electric bell uses an electromagnet and a striker on a spring.
  • Lamp (light) — converts electrical energy to light and heat. Indicator lamps (signal lights on control panels) and LED assemblies are output devices. LEDs are much more energy-efficient than filament lamps.

Choosing a Power Supply

The choice between mains and battery depends on four factors: power requirement, portability, safety and cost. A mains supply can deliver unlimited power continuously but requires fixed wiring and is dangerous if mishandled. Batteries are self-contained and portable but have a finite energy store and must be replaced or recharged. For safety reasons, all control electronics (sensors, microcontrollers, logic circuits) should operate at low DC voltages (typically 3.3–12 V) — mains AC must be stepped down and rectified before it can power them.

knowledge_checks.q: UK mains electricity is 230 V AC. What does the 'AC' mean?
options: The current flows in one direction only
The current reverses direction 50 times per second
The current is produced by a battery

knowledge_checks.q: What is the primary purpose of a relay in a control circuit?
options: To use a small control current to switch a large load current, with electrical isolation
To measure current in a circuit

knowledge_checks.q: A transformer that has more secondary turns than primary turns is called a step-_____ transformer and increases the output voltage.
A solenoid converts electrical energy into _____ mechanical motion.
Match each output device to the energy conversion it performs:
right: Electrical energy to rotary mechanical energy
Electrical energy to linear mechanical motion

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes alternating current (AC)?
A) Current that flows continuously in one direction only
B) Current that reverses direction many times per second, producing a sine wave
C) Current produced only by batteries
D) Current that is always at a fixed low voltage
practice_questions.marks: B) Current that reverses direction many times per second, producing a sine wave [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A step-down transformer has 3000 turns on the primary coil and is connected to a 230 V AC supply. The secondary coil has 150 turns.

Calculate the output voltage of the secondary coil.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns [1 mark]
Rearranged: Vs = Vp × Ns/Np = 230 × 150/3000 [1 mark for correct substitution]
= 11.5 V [1 mark for correct answer with unit]
[3 marks — method marks awarded even if arithmetic error]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using a battery power supply instead of a mains power supply in a portable engineering diagnostic tool.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct advantage, up to 2 marks:
- Batteries are portable — the tool can be used anywhere without needing a mains socket.
- Batteries produce DC directly, which electronic circuits require without additional conversion.
- Battery voltage is low (typically 3–12 V), making the device safer to handle than mains equipment.
- No mains cable required — the technician can move freely around a vehicle or machine.
[2 marks — vague answers like 'cheaper' or 'quicker' without context do not earn marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the function of a relay in an engineered system. Include in your answer:
(a) What the relay does
(b) Why electrical isolation between the two circuits is important
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
(a) A relay uses a small control current in an electromagnet/coil to attract an armature/switch contacts, which switches a separate circuit carrying a much larger current. [2 marks — 1 for 'small current controls large current', 1 for electromagnetic/physical mechanism]
(b) Isolation means the high-voltage/high-current power circuit (e.g. 230 V motor) is not electrically connected to the control circuit (e.g. 5 V microcontroller). This prevents high voltage damaging or destroying the sensitive control electronics. [2 marks — 1 for identifying the circuits as separate/not connected, 1 for consequence: protection of electronics]
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a motor and a solenoid as output devices in an engineering system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A motor converts electrical energy into continuous rotary motion; a solenoid converts electrical energy into a single linear push or pull motion.
- Motors are used where sustained rotation is needed (e.g. pump, conveyor); solenoids are used where a short, controlled linear stroke is needed (e.g. door lock, valve).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Elwick Automation Ltd designs a control system for an automated chemical-dosing pump. The pump motor runs on 230 V AC mains. The control circuit uses a microcontroller operating at 5 V DC.

Evaluate the use of a relay to interface the microcontroller with the pump motor. In your answer, consider at least one alternative approach.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Detailed explanation of the relay's function (small 5 V control signal drives coil, which switches the 230 V motor circuit). Evaluates advantages: electrical isolation protects the microcontroller from mains voltage, simple to implement, reliable, easily replaced. Evaluates disadvantages: relay switching is relatively slow (~10 ms), has moving parts that wear, produces a clicking noise. Considers an alternative (solid-state relay or TRIAC/thyristor): no moving parts, faster switching, silent, but more expensive and can fail silently without cutting power (safety concern in a chemical dosing context). Reaches a justified conclusion referencing the application.

Secure (5-6): Explains the isolation benefit clearly. Identifies at least one disadvantage and one alternative with some comparison. Conclusion present but may lack full engineering reasoning.

Developing (3-4): Describes relay function and one advantage. Limited alternative discussion.

Emerging (1-2): Basic relay description with minimal reasoning.

[8 marks]

lessons.title: Electronic Systems: Sensors, Logic and Components

practice_questions.text:
A student sees a component in a circuit diagram. It has three connections, with an arrow on one of them pointing outward.

Identify the component.
practice_questions.marks:
Transistor (NPN transistor) [1 mark]
Note: 'resistor' is a common wrong answer — resistors have two connections and are shown as a box or zigzag.

practice_questions.text:
Complete the truth table for an AND gate:

A | B | Output
0 | 0 | ___
0 | 1 | ___
1 | 0 | ___
1 | 1 | ___
practice_questions.marks:
0 | 0 | 0 [correct]
0 | 1 | 0 [correct]
1 | 0 | 0 [correct]
1 | 1 | 1 [correct]
1 marks awarded for each pair correct:
- Rows 1 and 2 correct [1 mark]
- Row 3 correct [1 mark]
- Row 4 correct [1 mark]
[3 marks total — must use 0 and 1 not yes/no or true/false]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an analogue signal and a digital signal. Give one example of a sensor that produces each type.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- Analogue signal: varies continuously between two values, can take any value (e.g. thermistor output, LDR output, microphone output).
- Digital signal: has only two states — HIGH (1) or LOW (0) (e.g. push-button switch, reed switch, digital encoder output).
[2 marks — must distinguish 'continuous range' vs 'two states' and give a valid example for each]

practice_questions.text:
A security alarm system uses two sensors: a door sensor (input A) and a motion sensor (input B). The alarm should sound only when both sensors are triggered at the same time.

(a) Name the logic gate that should be used.
(b) Complete the truth table for this system.
(c) Explain why an OR gate would not be suitable.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
(a) AND gate [1 mark]
(b) Truth table:
A=0,B=0 → 0; A=0,B=1 → 0; A=1,B=0 → 0; A=1,B=1 → 1 [1 mark for all rows correct]
(c) An OR gate output is HIGH when either A OR B is triggered alone — the alarm would sound even if only one sensor is triggered, causing false alarms. [2 marks — 1 for identifying OR would activate on a single sensor, 1 for linking to the consequence (false alarms)]
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: State the function of an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) and explain where it is positioned in a programmable electronic system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- An ADC converts a continuous analogue voltage (from a sensor) into a discrete digital binary number.
- It is placed between the analogue sensor and the microcontroller/digital processor, so that the sensor output can be read by the digital system.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Fenwick Electronic Systems Ltd is designing a temperature-monitoring unit for a food refrigeration cabinet. The unit must trigger an alarm if the temperature rises above 5°C. The system uses a thermistor, an ADC, a microcontroller and a buzzer.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using a thermistor as the temperature-sensing element for this application. In your answer, consider at least one alternative sensor.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Explains how a thermistor (NTC) produces an analogue voltage that decreases as resistance falls with rising temperature; this must be converted by an ADC before the microcontroller can process it. Evaluates advantages (cheap, small, robust, wide temperature range, fast response). Evaluates disadvantages (non-linear response — resistance doesn't drop proportionally with temperature, requires calibration; analogue output needs ADC). Considers an alternative (digital temperature sensor IC such as DS18B20): direct digital output (no ADC needed), pre-calibrated, higher accuracy. Compares on cost, accuracy, integration complexity and food-safety regulatory context. Justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6): Correct description of thermistor function, at least two advantages and one disadvantage, one alternative with brief comparison. Conclusion present.

Developing (3-4): Basic description of thermistor. One advantage and one disadvantage. Limited alternative.

Emerging (1-2): Simple identification of thermistor with minimal reasoning.

[8 marks]

before.content_html:
What Is a Microcontroller?

A microcontroller is a small computer on a single chip. It contains a processor (to execute instructions), memory (to store the program and data) and a set of input and output connections — all on one integrated circuit. Microcontrollers run a program that reads sensor inputs, makes decisions and drives output devices. They replace large banks of discrete logic gates, making control systems compact, flexible and reprogrammable.

Common microcontroller families include the PIC (Peripheral Interface Controller — widely used in industrial and automotive applications) and development boards such as the BBC micro:bit and Arduino (used in school workshops and rapid prototyping). For the purposes of this specification, the key rule is that a microcontroller is limited to three inputs and three outputs within an engineered system — this keeps the design manageable at GCSE level.

Key Fact

The microcontroller follows the input–process–output model. Sensors and switches are inputs; the microcontroller’s program is the process; actuators (motors, solenoids, LEDs, buzzers) are outputs. The program runs in a continuous loop: read inputs → make decision → set outputs → repeat.

Flowchart Programming

Microcontrollers are typically programmed using a flowchart program at GCSE level. A flowchart shows exactly what the microcontroller does at each step, making it easy to trace the logic before writing code. The standard symbols are the same four shapes from Lesson 1: oval (start/stop), rectangle (process), parallelogram (input/output) and diamond (decision).

A typical microcontroller flowchart for a temperature-controlled fan looks like this in sequence:

  1. START
  2. Read temperature sensor (ADC converts analogue output to digital number)
  3. Decision: is temperature above threshold (e.g. 30°C)?
  4. YES → Switch fan motor ON; loop back to “Read temperature sensor”
  5. NO → Switch fan motor OFF; loop back to “Read temperature sensor”

This loop runs continuously while the system is powered. The decision diamond and its YES/NO branches create the responsive behaviour. Changing the threshold value in the program immediately changes the system behaviour — no rewiring needed. This is a key advantage of programmable systems over fixed logic-gate circuits.

Discrete logic gates are fixed — once a circuit is built, its behaviour is determined by the physical wiring. Adding a new condition means redesigning and rebuilding the circuit. A microcontroller replaces all the logic gates with a program, so:

  • Behaviour can be changed by reprogramming — no hardware changes needed.
  • Multiple conditions and complex decision trees can be handled by a single chip that would require dozens of logic gates if built from discrete components.
  • The same hardware platform (e.g. Arduino) can be programmed to control a fan, a door lock or a conveyor — reducing component variety and manufacturing cost.
  • Timing functions (delays, PWM motor speed control) are built into the microcontroller — they would require separate timer ICs in a discrete circuit.

The ADC and Sensor Thresholds

Most real-world sensors (thermistors, LDRs, pressure transducers) produce analogue sensor outputs. The microcontroller’s internal ADC converts these to a digital number (typically 0–1023 for a 10-bit ADC). The program then compares this number to a sensor threshold: if the reading exceeds the threshold, the output is triggered; if not, it stays off.

Example: an LDR connected to a 10-bit ADC produces values from 0 (very dark) to 1023 (very bright). The program might set a threshold of 200: if reading < 200, switch on the lamp; if reading ≥ 200, switch off. Adjusting the threshold changes the light level at which the lamp triggers, without any soldering.

Key Fact

A sensor threshold is a number stored in the microcontroller program. The ADC converts the analogue sensor voltage into a digital value; the program compares this to the threshold and decides what action to take. Changing the threshold changes the system’s sensitivity without rewiring — this is a major advantage of programmable control over fixed logic.

Microcontroller output pins supply only a small current (typically 20–40 mA). Most actuators (motors, solenoids, lamps) draw far more current than this. Connecting a motor directly to an output pin would damage or destroy the microcontroller. An interfacing component is used to switch the larger current safely.

The two main interfacing components are:

  • Bipolar junction transistor (BJT) — a small base current from the microcontroller controls a much larger collector-to-emitter current through the load. Think of it as a current-controlled switch. An NPN transistor is used with the load between the positive supply and the collector, and the emitter to ground.
  • Field-effect transistor (FET/MOSFET) — a voltage on the gate terminal switches a much larger current through the drain-to-source path. FETs are voltage-controlled (not current-controlled like BJTs) and are preferred for driving motors and high-power LEDs because they can switch rapidly and waste very little energy when fully on.

A protection diode (flyback diode) is placed across an inductive load (motor, solenoid) in parallel to absorb the voltage spike that occurs when the device is switched off. Without it, the spike can destroy the transistor or FET.

Industrial Application: Pick-and-Place Machines

A pick-and-place machine on an electronics production line uses a microcontroller to control three outputs: a vacuum gripper (picks up components), an X-Y positioning motor (moves to target location) and a placement actuator (releases the component). Three sensors (position encoder, component-present sensor, placement-complete sensor) provide the three inputs. The microcontroller loops through its flowchart program hundreds of times per second, precisely coordinating all six connections. This is exactly the three-inputs, three-outputs model described in the specification.

Which one of the following best describes a microcontroller?
A) A type of logic gate used to invert a signal
B) A single chip containing a processor, memory and programmable I/O connections
C) A relay that switches between mains and battery power
D) A sensor that converts temperature to a digital signal
practice_questions.marks: B) A single chip containing a processor, memory and programmable I/O connections [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A microcontroller is used in an automatic plant-watering system. A soil moisture sensor is the input; a water pump motor is the output.

The system must switch the pump ON when the moisture reading falls below a set threshold, and switch it OFF when the reading is at or above the threshold.

Draw and label a flowchart for this system. Your flowchart must include: START, reading the sensor, a decision, switching the pump on or off, and a loop back.
practice_questions.type: 5 marks — Complete the Flowchart or System Diagram
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for:
- START terminator (oval) present [1 mark]
- 'Read soil moisture sensor' in a rectangle or parallelogram, with correct placement [1 mark]
- Decision diamond: 'Is moisture below threshold?' (or equivalent) with YES and NO branches [1 mark]
- YES branch: 'Switch pump ON'; NO branch: 'Switch pump OFF' (or vice versa — check logic is consistent) [1 mark]
- Feedback loop back to 'Read sensor' from both branches (continuous control loop) [1 mark]
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using a microcontroller to control an automated system instead of using a fixed logic gate circuit.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per advantage, up to 2 marks:
- A microcontroller can be reprogrammed to change its behaviour without rewiring or replacing hardware.
- A single microcontroller can handle many inputs and outputs with complex decision logic that would require numerous discrete logic gate ICs.
- Built-in timing and ADC functions remove the need for separate timer ICs and converter chips.
- The same microcontroller hardware can be reused for different products by changing only the program.
[2 marks — vague answers like 'easier' without specifying the mechanism do not earn marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a transistor or FET is needed between a microcontroller output pin and a DC motor. In your answer, refer to current.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A microcontroller output pin can only supply a small current (typically 20-40 mA), which is not enough to drive a motor.
- A transistor or FET is used as a switch: a small control current/voltage on the base/gate switches a much larger current through the motor.
- Without the interfacing component, the large motor current would damage or destroy the microcontroller.
[2 marks — must mention small control current vs large motor current]

practice_questions.text:
A light-sensing system uses an LDR, a microcontroller and an LED indicator. The LDR is connected to the microcontroller via an ADC. The system must switch the LED on when light levels are low.

Describe the four stages that happen between the LDR detecting a change in light level and the LED switching on.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct stage, up to 4 marks:
1. The LDR resistance increases as light falls, changing the analogue voltage in the sensing circuit.
2. The ADC converts this analogue voltage into a digital number (e.g. 0-1023).
3. The microcontroller program compares the digital number to the stored threshold value.
4. If the reading is below the threshold, the program sets the output pin HIGH, which switches the LED on (via a transistor/directly if current is within limit).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Aethon Robotics is designing an automated greenhouse monitoring system. The system monitors temperature and humidity using two analogue sensors, and controls a heating element, a ventilation fan and a misting pump. The lead engineer proposes using a microcontroller rather than separate logic gate circuits for each function.

Evaluate this proposal. Consider advantages and disadvantages of using a microcontroller for this application.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Detailed evaluation. Advantages: single chip handles all three output devices and two sensor inputs (within the three-inputs/three-outputs model if temperature and humidity are the two active inputs); reprogrammable — thresholds and timing can be adjusted for different crops without hardware changes; built-in ADC converts analogue sensor outputs; timing control allows delays (e.g. fan runs for 30 s after triggering). Disadvantages: program must be written and tested; if the microcontroller fails, all three functions stop; needs correct interfacing components for high-current actuators (heater, fan, pump). Compares with discrete approach (very complex wiring, not reprogrammable, harder to modify). Reaches justified conclusion referencing the greenhouse context.

Secure (5-6): Identifies key advantages (reprogrammable, handles multiple I/O) and at least one disadvantage. Some comparison with alternative. Conclusion present.

Developing (3-4): Describes microcontroller function and one or two advantages. Limited evaluation depth.

Emerging (1-2): Basic description of what a microcontroller is with minimal evaluative comment.

[8 marks]

before.content_html:
Forces on Structures

Every structure must support and transmit loads — the forces acting on it. Engineers classify loads into two main categories. A dead load is the permanent weight of the structure itself (the steel frame of a bridge, the concrete deck). A live load (also called an imposed load) changes over time — the vehicles crossing a bridge, the people standing on a floor, the goods stacked in a warehouse.

A dynamic load is applied suddenly or changes rapidly — a machine vibrating at high speed, a vehicle braking sharply, an impact during a crash. Dynamic loads are often more damaging than static loads of the same magnitude because the rapid change creates additional stress within the material.

Key Fact

Dead load = permanent weight of the structure (e.g. steel beams, concrete slab). Live load = variable load from use (e.g. vehicles, people, stored goods). Dynamic load = suddenly applied or rapidly changing force (e.g. impact, machine vibration). Cables in a suspension bridge carry tension — NOT compression. This is a common exam error.

Types of Internal Force

When a load is applied to a structural member, it creates internal forces. You need to identify five types:

  • Tension — a pulling force that stretches a member. Cables, suspension bridge hangers and tent guy-ropes are in tension. Cables can only carry tension; they buckle and go slack under compression.
  • Compression — a pushing force that squeezes a member. Stone arch bridges, concrete columns and walls are in compression. Brittle materials (concrete, stone, brick) are strong in compression but weak in tension.
  • Bending — a force that causes a member to curve. A beam supported at both ends and loaded in the middle bends, putting the top surface in compression and the bottom surface in tension.
  • Torsion — a twisting force along a shaft’s axis. A car driveshaft experiences torsion as it transmits engine torque to the wheels.
  • Buckling — sudden sideways collapse of a long, slender compression member (column or strut) under compressive load. A thin aluminium column buckles before the material crushes in compression.

A space frame is a three-dimensional framework of interconnected bars arranged in triangles. The triangle is the only shape that is inherently rigid without requiring rigid joints — any force applied to a triangle is resolved into tension or compression along the members. Electricity pylons, roof trusses and racing car roll cages are all space frames.

A monocoque structure carries loads through its outer skin rather than an internal frame. Monocoque is French for “single shell.” Aircraft fuselages and Formula 1 carbon fibre chassis are monocoque — the shell itself provides rigidity and strength without a separate skeleton inside. This produces very low weight for a given stiffness.

Pascal’s Law and Pressure Systems

Pneumatic and hydraulic systems both use fluid (gas or liquid) under pressure to transmit force. The underlying principle is Pascal’s law: pressure applied at one point in a sealed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid. This means a force applied at a small piston can produce a much larger force at a larger piston — force amplification.

The pressure equation is: $$P = \frac{F}{A}$$ where \(P\) is pressure in pascals (Pa), \(F\) is force in newtons (N) and \(A\) is area in square metres (m2). Because pressure is equal throughout a sealed fluid, we can write: $$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$ where subscript 1 is the input piston and subscript 2 is the output piston. Rearranging: $$F_2 = F_1 \times \frac{A_2}{A_1}$$

Key Fact

Pascal’s law: pressure in an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Force amplification: \(F_2 = F_1 \times \frac{A_2}{A_1}\). A hydraulic system with an output piston ten times larger than the input piston produces ten times the output force. The trade-off: the output piston moves a much shorter distance than the input piston (the fluid volume is conserved).

Pneumatic vs Hydraulic Systems

Both systems use fluids under pressure, but the type of fluid determines the application:

  • Pneumatic systems use compressed air. Air is compressible, so pneumatic systems act quickly but cannot sustain very high forces. They are clean (no fluid spills), cheap to run (air is free) and safe in food and pharmaceutical environments. Typical applications: robot grippers, packaging machines, pneumatic drills, spray painting robots, door openers on trains.
  • Hydraulic systems use hydraulic fluid (oil). Liquids are virtually incompressible, which means the force transmitted is very precise and very high. Hydraulic systems can produce enormous forces in compact cylinders. Applications: JCB excavator arms, car brake systems, aircraft landing gear, forklift truck mast, heavy press machines.

A double-acting cylinder has two air inlets — one on each side of the piston. Compressed air directed to the back drives the piston forward (extend); air directed to the front drives it back (retract). This gives positive force in both directions, unlike a single-acting cylinder that uses a spring to retract.

A 5/2 directional control valve is the standard valve used to control a double-acting cylinder. The “5” means five ports (air inlet, two cylinder ports, two exhaust ports); the “2” means two switching positions (extend or retract). Shifting the valve from one position to the other sends compressed air to one side of the cylinder and vents the other side to exhaust. In an automated system, the 5/2 valve is actuated electrically (a solenoid moves the spool inside the valve) rather than manually.

Worked Calculation: Force Amplification

Daleside Pumps manufactures a hydraulic press for forming sheet steel. The input piston has an area of 0.002 m2. The output piston has an area of 0.04 m2. The operator applies a force of 150 N to the input piston. Calculate the output force.

$$F_2 = F_1 \times \frac{A_2}{A_1} = 150 \times \frac{0.04}{0.002} = 150 \times 20 = 3000\text{ N}$$ The hydraulic press amplifies the input force by a factor of 20, producing 3000 N at the output piston. Note: the output piston moves 20 times less distance than the input piston (volume is conserved).

A hydraulic car jack has an input piston with an area of 0.005 m² and an output piston with an area of 0.05 m². The mechanic applies a force of 200 N to the input piston.

Calculate the output force produced by the jack.

Substitution: F2 = 200 × 0.05/0.005 [1 mark]
= 200 × 10 [1 mark for correct ratio]

practice_questions.text: Give two differences between a pneumatic system and a hydraulic system. For each difference, explain how it affects the choice of system for a particular engineering application.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clear differences, each with an application-linked explanation:
- Pneumatic uses compressible air (fast-acting, lower maximum force); hydraulic uses incompressible oil (precise, very high force). Example: pneumatic for robot grippers and packaging machines where speed matters; hydraulic for excavator arms and car brakes where high force or precision is critical.
- Pneumatic is cleaner (no risk of oil leaks); hydraulic risk of fluid contamination. Example: pneumatic preferred in food/pharma environments; hydraulic acceptable in outdoor heavy plant.
- Pneumatic cylinders extend quickly due to air compression; hydraulic extends more slowly but with greater control.
Both differences must explicitly link to an application.

Secure (3-4): Two differences identified with partial application links. May lack specificity in the application context.

Developing (2): One difference with a brief application link.

Emerging (1): One difference named with no application link.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the function of a 5/2 directional control valve in a pneumatic circuit that controls a double-acting cylinder.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A 5/2 valve has five ports (air inlet, two cylinder ports, two exhaust ports) and two switching positions.
- Switching from one position to the other directs compressed air to one side of the cylinder (extending the piston) while venting the other side to exhaust, and vice versa when switched back (retracting the piston).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Marrowbone Engineering manufactures industrial clamping equipment. The design team must choose between a pneumatic clamping system and a hydraulic clamping system for a new metal-forming press that must apply a clamping force of 50,000 N.

Evaluate which system is better suited to this application. In your answer, refer to Pascal's law and the properties of the fluids involved.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Explains Pascal's law (pressure transmitted equally in enclosed fluid, allowing force amplification via F2 = F1 × A2/A1). Shows that both systems can amplify force, but a 50,000 N requirement is very high. Evaluates hydraulic: oil is incompressible — force is transmitted precisely and consistently at very high levels; force amplification is reliable and predictable; used in heavy presses and brakes for these reasons; disadvantage: oil leak risk, higher cost, maintenance of seals. Evaluates pneumatic: air is compressible — force output fluctuates slightly with air consumption; achieving 50,000 N with air pressure alone would require very large cylinder area or very high operating pressure (safety concern); advantage: cleaner, cheaper. Concludes hydraulic is more appropriate for this application with clear reasoning.

Secure (5-6): Correctly identifies hydraulic as better for high-force application. Mentions incompressibility of hydraulic fluid and compressibility of air. Some reference to force amplification principle. Conclusion present with reasoning.

Developing (3-4): States hydraulic is better with a partial explanation of why. May mention force amplification without linking it to fluid compressibility.

Emerging (1-2): Identifies one of the two systems with minimal reasoning.

[8 marks]
